title: Rune-frequency entropy: balance without order
summary: Calculate empirical Shannon entropy from archived rune counts, reproduce LP2-31, and understand what this measurement cannot distinguish.
html:
Single-rune entropy summarizes a frequency distribution. It is low when most observations belong to a few symbols and higher when observations are spread more evenly. It does not inspect the order of the runes. Use it beside IoC as a descriptive measurement, not as a test that a page is encrypted or random.

From counts to bits

Let N be the number of retained runes and c be one rune’s count. Its empirical probability is p = c/N. Compute H = −sum(p × log2(p)) over nonzero counts. A zero count contributes zero; do not attempt to evaluate log2(0). Base-two logarithms give bits per symbol. This is the Shannon-entropy formula applied to observed frequencies; SciPy’s entropy reference documents the formula and logarithm-base convention. The script here uses Python’s standard library.

Invented inputCountsEntropy
AAAAAAAA80 bits
AAAABBBB4, 41 bit
ABABABAB4, 41 bit
AABBCCDD2, 2, 2, 22 bits
AAAB3, 1About 0.811278 bits

For two equally frequent symbols, each contributes −0.5 × log2(0.5) = 0.5; their total is 1. Notice that grouping and alternating the same four A and four B symbols changes nothing. Neither does consistently renaming A and B. The statistic summarizes the counts, not the arrangement.

Reproduce a manuscript measurement

Extract the reference-data bundle, keeping its folders together, and run:

python scripts/rune_entropy.py lp2-31
python scripts/rune_entropy.py lp2-31 --output lp2-31-entropy.json

The script uses the same counting implementation as the IoC report: archived runes, including rune headings; no corrections or decryption. Punctuation, spaces, Latin text and printed decimal numbers are excluded. The saved UTF-8 JSON contains the source hash, alphabet hash, ordered counts, sample size and result. Existing output files are not replaced. No network or AI request is made.

LP2-31: what the result says

FieldResult
Retained runes269
Distinct observed runes29
Empirical entropy4.814030217724328 bits per rune
Exactly uniform 29-symbol distributionlog2(29) ≈ 4.857980995127572 bits per rune

The measurement uses the archived LP2-31 transcription, SHA-256 493cb51478b106dd626ff93625abaf10c9675ad221896b5206809041dfd55b68. Its frequency distribution is fairly even under this counting rule. Closeness to the uniform value is not a probability, confidence score or identification of the cipher.

The uniform value is a distributional upper bound, not the expected measured value of a finite random page. Here 269 is not divisible by 29, so exact equality of all integer counts is impossible. Sample length and the number of observed symbols matter when comparing pages. An empty rune stream receives null, because there are no empirical probabilities to calculate; it should not be mistaken for a nonempty one-symbol stream with entropy zero.

The most even counts this length permits

For 269 runes in a 29-rune alphabet, divide 269 = 29 × 9 + 8. The most even possible counts are eight symbols appearing ten times and twenty-one appearing nine times. Their entropy is 4.856331980164111 bits per rune. The report includes this as finite_sample_maximum_entropy_bits.

In general, write N = Kq + r, where K is the alphabet size and r is the remainder. Assign count q + 1 to r symbols and q to the other K − r symbols, then apply the entropy formula. Moving one observation from a count that exceeds another by at least two makes the counts more balanced and increases entropy; repeating this gives the maximum. This is a bound across all possible count vectors of that length, not a rearrangement of the page’s actual counts.

Sample length, alphabet of 29Maximizing countsMaximum empirical entropy
1One count of 1; 28 zeros0 bits
4Four counts of 1; 25 zeros2 bits
5829 counts of 2log2(29) bits
269Eight counts of 10; 21 counts of 9About 4.856332 bits

The alphabet remains all 29 runes, even if a short sample contains fewer distinct runes. Neither this maximum nor the gap below it is an expected random value or a significance test. Random sampling can produce uneven counts; a probability claim needs a specified null model. Empty input has no empirical distribution, so its maximum is also reported as null.

Why random samples need not reach the maximum

Imagine a source that independently emits A or B with equal probability. Its underlying distribution has entropy 1 bit. Now take just two symbols. There are four equally likely ordered samples:

SampleObserved countsEmpirical entropy
AA2, 00 bits
AB1, 11 bit
BA1, 11 bit
BB0, 20 bits

The average measured entropy is (0 + 1 + 1 + 0) / 4 = 0.5 bits. That is below both the source’s entropy and the maximum empirical entropy attainable with two symbols. Yet every sample was produced by the same independent, balanced source. No measurement error or hidden pattern was needed to create the gap.

The distinction is between a source distribution and the frequencies in one finite sample. With only two draws, a symbol can be missing simply because it did not occur. The empirical formula assigns that unobserved symbol probability zero even though its probability under the stipulated source remains one half.

Enumerate the example

from itertools import product
from collections import Counter
from math import log2

values = []
for sample in product("AB", repeat=2):
    counts = Counter(sample).values()
    h = sum(-(c / 2) * log2(c / 2) for c in counts)
    values.append(h)
    print("".join(sample), f"{h:.1f}")
print("Mean:", sum(values) / len(values))

The final line is Mean: 0.5. This exact enumeration assumes equal probabilities for all four samples. A model that fixes the counts at one A and one B permits only AB and BA, both with entropy 1. Those are different models: random sampling allows the counts to change, while shuffling a fixed page does not.

For manuscript comparisons, preserve the sample length, alphabet, and proposed sampling rule. The toy example explains the distinction; it does not assign a probability to LP2-31’s entropy or establish that its runes were generated independently. See null models and selection before treating a shortfall from the maximum as evidence about a cipher.

Can two texts have the same IoC but different entropy?

Yes. Both measurements use symbol frequencies, but they compress those frequencies in different ways. IoC counts matching pairs; entropy uses logarithms of the observed proportions. One score does not generally determine the other.

Compare these two invented six-symbol strings. They are teaching examples, not manuscript readings. Their lengths and matching-pair totals are identical:

InputCountsIoCEntropy
AAABBB3, 32/51 bit
AAAABC4, 1, 12/5About 1.251629 bits

The matching-pair totals are 3 × 2 + 3 × 2 = 12 and 4 × 3 + 1 × 0 + 1 × 0 = 12. Each string has 6 × 5 = 30 ordered pairs of distinct positions, so both IoCs are 12/30 = 2/5.

The second string contains a more dominant symbol, but also two less frequent alternatives instead of one. Its entropy is higher, while IoC ties. Sorting pages by entropy therefore need not produce the reverse of their IoC ranking. Higher entropy here does not establish a better decryption, more meaningful text or a more secure cipher.

Check the comparison

Run this self-contained Python example. It calculates IoC as an exact fraction and entropy with base-two logarithms:

from collections import Counter
from fractions import Fraction
from math import log2

for text in ("AAABBB", "AAAABC"):
    counts = Counter(text).values()
    n = len(text)
    ioc = Fraction(sum(c * (c - 1) for c in counts), n * (n - 1))
    entropy = -sum((c / n) * log2(c / n) for c in counts)
    print(text, "IoC:", ioc, "entropy:", f"{entropy:.6f}")

Expected output:

AAABBB IoC: 2/5 entropy: 1.000000
AAAABC IoC: 2/5 entropy: 1.251629

Adding the 26 or 27 unused runes to the count array changes neither result: zero counts contribute nothing. Both examples therefore fit within the same 29-symbol alphabet. Their order can be rearranged without changing either score. For selecting candidate transformations, consult which properties each operation preserves; for interpreting an unusual value, specify a comparison model.

Matching symbols: with or without replacement?

Choose one position uniformly from a text of N symbols, then choose a second position. If the second choice can select the first position again, the probability of a matching symbol is C = sum((c/N)²). This is sampling with replacement. If the positions must be different, the matching probability is the IoC used in this wiki: I = sum(c(c−1)) / (N(N−1)).

The difference is the possibility of selecting the same position twice, which always produces a match. For N greater than one:

Separate the squared counts
sum(c²) = sum(c(c−1)) + N
Divide by N²
C = 1/N + ((N−1)/N) × I
Recover IoC
I = (N × C − 1) / (N−1)

See every possible pair

For AAABBB, C is 1/2 but IoC is 2/5. If all N symbols are different, IoC is zero while C is 1/N: the only matching draws with replacement are those that revisit the same position. A one-symbol text has C = 1, but its IoC is undefined because there is no pair of distinct positions.

A lower bound on Shannon entropy

The same empirical probabilities give a useful mathematical check: H ≥ −log2(C). To see why, select a symbol using its observed probability p. Shannon entropy is the average of −log2(p); the average of p under that selection is sum(p²) = C. The function −log2 is convex, so its average cannot be below its value at the average. Equality holds when all observed symbols have equal probabilities.

This is a bound, not a conversion formula for entropy. The two six-symbol examples above have the same C = 1/2 and therefore the same bound of 1 bit, but their entropies differ. Do not insert IoC directly into the logarithm: it uses a different sampling rule and can be zero even for a nonempty text.

Check LP2-31 using exact fractions

For the 269-rune stream above, the matching ordered-pair count is 2,376. This short calculation reproduces the conversion:

from fractions import Fraction
from math import log2

n = 269
ioc = Fraction(2376, n * (n - 1))
collision = Fraction(1, n) + Fraction(n - 1, n) * ioc
print("With replacement:", collision)
print("Entropy lower bound:", f"{-log2(float(collision)):.6f}")

Expected output:

With replacement: 2645/72361
Entropy lower bound: 4.773873

The measured Shannon entropy, about 4.814030 bits, is above this bound. Both values describe this count distribution. Neither is a probability that the page is random or evidence for a particular cipher. Use the null-model guide for that separate question.

What it cannot distinguish

A pure transposition preserves every count, so it preserves this entropy. A fixed one-to-one substitution relabels the same counts and also preserves it. Therefore this score cannot choose among those transformations of the same input. See cipher invariants.

This is not an entropy-rate estimate: it does not model how a symbol depends on preceding symbols. The alternating example above has a predictable pattern despite its balanced counts. Use repeated sequences to inspect adjacency, and specify a comparison model before claiming statistical surprise. A frequency summary alone does not measure meaning, compressibility under a particular compressor, or resistance to cryptanalysis.

Files and verification

Entropy script · small-example tests · shared counting implementation. The worked result was calculated from the archived source on 20 October 2026. The examples check known distributions, order invariance, input validation and the empty-page case. This is a descriptive method guide, not a published experiment on a candidate solution.

	Sample	Observed counts	Empirical entropy
	AA	2, 0	0 bits
	AB	1, 1	1 bit
	BA	1, 1	1 bit
	BB	0, 2	0 bits

The average measured entropy is (0 + 1 + 1 + 0) / 4 = 0.5 bits. That is below both the source’s entropy and the maximum empirical entropy attainable with two symbols. Yet every sample was produced by the same independent, balanced source. No measurement error or hidden pattern was needed to create the gap.

The distinction is between a source distribution and the frequencies in one finite sample. With only two draws, a symbol can be missing simply because it did not occur. The empirical formula assigns that unobserved symbol probability zero even though its probability under the stipulated source remains one half.

Enumerate the example

from itertools import product
from collections import Counter
from math import log2

values = []
for sample in product("AB", repeat=2):
    counts = Counter(sample).values()
    h = sum(-(c / 2) * log2(c / 2) for c in counts)
    values.append(h)
    print("".join(sample), f"{h:.1f}")
print("Mean:", sum(values) / len(values))

The final line is Mean: 0.5. This exact enumeration assumes equal probabilities for all four samples. A model that fixes the counts at one A and one B permits only AB and BA, both with entropy 1. Those are different models: random sampling allows the counts to change, while shuffling a fixed page does not.

For manuscript comparisons, preserve the sample length, alphabet, and proposed sampling rule. The toy example explains the distinction; it does not assign a probability to LP2-31’s entropy or establish that its runes were generated independently. See null models and selection before treating a shortfall from the maximum as evidence about a cipher.

Can two texts have the same IoC but different entropy?

Yes. Both measurements use symbol frequencies, but they compress those frequencies in different ways. IoC counts matching pairs; entropy uses logarithms of the observed proportions. One score does not generally determine the other.

Compare these two invented six-symbol strings. They are teaching examples, not manuscript readings. Their lengths and matching-pair totals are identical:

	Input	Counts	IoC	Entropy

	AAABBB	3, 3	2/5	1 bit

	AAAABC	4, 1, 1	2/5	About 1.251629 bits


The matching-pair totals are 3 × 2 + 3 × 2 = 12 and 4 × 3 + 1 × 0 + 1 × 0 = 12. Each string has 6 × 5 = 30 ordered pairs of distinct positions, so both IoCs are 12/30 = 2/5.

The second string contains a more dominant symbol, but also two less frequent alternatives instead of one. Its entropy is higher, while IoC ties. Sorting pages by entropy therefore need not produce the reverse of their IoC ranking. Higher entropy here does not establish a better decryption, more meaningful text or a more secure cipher.

Check the comparison

Run this self-contained Python example. It calculates IoC as an exact fraction and entropy with base-two logarithms:

from collections import Counter
from fractions import Fraction
from math import log2

for text in ("AAABBB", "AAAABC"):
    counts = Counter(text).values()
    n = len(text)
    ioc = Fraction(sum(c * (c - 1) for c in counts), n * (n - 1))
    entropy = -sum((c / n) * log2(c / n) for c in counts)
    print(text, "IoC:", ioc, "entropy:", f"{entropy:.6f}")

Expected output:

AAABBB IoC: 2/5 entropy: 1.000000
AAAABC IoC: 2/5 entropy: 1.251629

Adding the 26 or 27 unused runes to the count array changes neither result: zero counts contribute nothing. Both examples therefore fit within the same 29-symbol alphabet. Their order can be rearranged without changing either score. For selecting candidate transformations, consult which properties each operation preserves; for interpreting an unusual value, specify a comparison model.

Matching symbols: with or without replacement?

Choose one position uniformly from a text of N symbols, then choose a second position. If the second choice can select the first position again, the probability of a matching symbol is C = sum((c/N)²). This is sampling with replacement. If the positions must be different, the matching probability is the IoC used in this wiki: I = sum(c(c−1)) / (N(N−1)).

The difference is the possibility of selecting the same position twice, which always produces a match. For N greater than one:

Separate the squared counts
sum(c²) = sum(c(c−1)) + N
Divide by N²
C = 1/N + ((N−1)/N) × I
Recover IoC
I = (N × C − 1) / (N−1)

See every possible pair

[Image: A six-by-six grid for AAABBB: 18 cells match symbols, including six crossed same-position cells. Removing the diagonal leaves 12 matches among 30 pairs.]
Every cell selects a first and second position. A blue dot marks equal symbols; a cross marks reuse of the same position. Open full size · Download SVG. Invented example, not manuscript data.

For AAABBB, C is 1/2 but IoC is 2/5. If all N symbols are different, IoC is zero while C is 1/N: the only matching draws with replacement are those that revisit the same position. A one-symbol text has C = 1, but its IoC is undefined because there is no pair of distinct positions.

A lower bound on Shannon entropy

The same empirical probabilities give a useful mathematical check: H ≥ −log2(C). To see why, select a symbol using its observed probability p. Shannon entropy is the average of −log2(p); the average of p under that selection is sum(p²) = C. The function −log2 is convex, so its average cannot be below its value at the average. Equality holds when all observed symbols have equal probabilities.

This is a bound, not a conversion formula for entropy. The two six-symbol examples above have the same C = 1/2 and therefore the same bound of 1 bit, but their entropies differ. Do not insert IoC directly into the logarithm: it uses a different sampling rule and can be zero even for a nonempty text.

Check LP2-31 using exact fractions

For the 269-rune stream above, the matching ordered-pair count is 2,376. This short calculation reproduces the conversion:

from fractions import Fraction
from math import log2

n = 269
ioc = Fraction(2376, n * (n - 1))
collision = Fraction(1, n) + Fraction(n - 1, n) * ioc
print("With replacement:", collision)
print("Entropy lower bound:", f"{-log2(float(collision)):.6f}")

Expected output:

With replacement: 2645/72361
Entropy lower bound: 4.773873

The measured Shannon entropy, about 4.814030 bits, is above this bound. Both values describe this count distribution. Neither is a probability that the page is random or evidence for a particular cipher. Use the null-model guide for that separate question.

What it cannot distinguish

A pure transposition preserves every count, so it preserves this entropy. A fixed one-to-one substitution relabels the same counts and also preserves it. Therefore this score cannot choose among those transformations of the same input. See cipher invariants.

This is not an entropy-rate estimate: it does not model how a symbol depends on preceding symbols. The alternating example above has a predictable pattern despite its balanced counts. Use repeated sequences to inspect adjacency, and specify a comparison model before claiming statistical surprise. A frequency summary alone does not measure meaning, compressibility under a particular compressor, or resistance to cryptanalysis.

Files and verification

Entropy script · small-example tests · shared counting implementation. The worked result was calculated from the archived source on 20 October 2026. The examples check known distributions, order invariance, input validation and the empty-page case. This is a descriptive method guide, not a published experiment on a candidate solution.

title: Repeated rune sequences: bigrams and trigrams
summary: Locate overlapping repeats, reproduce exact counts and rune positions, and distinguish repetition from a cipher claim.
html:
An n-gram is a sequence of n consecutive symbols. A bigram contains two; a trigram contains three. Counting repeated rune n-grams lets you ask which exact sequences recur and where. Unlike a whole-page index of coincidence, this measurement depends on neighboring symbols and their order.

Slide a window, one rune at a time

For the synthetic stream F–U–F–U–F, a three-rune window has three possible starting positions:

Start, from zeroWindowIncluded positions
0F–U–F0, 1, 2
1U–F–U1, 2, 3
2F–U–F2, 3, 4

F–U–F is one repeated pattern with two occurrences, starting at 0 and 2. The occurrences share position 2: this procedure counts overlapping windows. Similarly, F–F–F–F contains three overlapping F–F windows, not two. For N runes and a positive window length n, the number of windows is max(0, N − n + 1).

Exactly which stream is counted

The supplied script reads one archived transcription and retains the 29 alphabet runes in source order, including headings. It removes every non-rune: punctuation, spaces, line markers and printed decimal numbers. Windows can therefore cross word, line and paragraph boundaries. They never cross into another page.

This is a rune-stream measurement, not a count of repeated words or preserved visual rows. Removing a separator makes the runes on its two sides adjacent. A study limited to words, rows or body text would need different segmentation and should not be reported as the same test. Unknown characters in the Runic Unicode block cause an error rather than disappearing silently.

Reproduce the report

Use the repository or reference-data bundle; see setup instructions. Python 3 and its standard library are sufficient. The commands read local files and do not use AI or network services.

python scripts/rune_ngrams.py lp2-31 --length 2
python scripts/rune_ngrams.py lp2-31 --length 3
python scripts/rune_ngrams.py lp2-31 --length 2 --output lp2-31-bigrams.json

The output is UTF-8 JSON with the actual runes visible in its strings. Terminal output and the saved report use the same LF line endings. A terminal font without Runic characters may show boxes; inspect the saved UTF-8 file in a suitable editor rather than replacing the symbols. Length defaults to 3 and accepts integers from 1 through 12. An existing output file is never replaced. A page with no archived rune transcription produces an explanatory error.

Each report records the source file’s SHA-256, the complete ordered alphabet and its SHA-256, the filtering rule, rune count, total windows and every pattern occurring at least twice. Each pattern includes its rune indices, Latin labels, count and starting positions. Starts are zero-based rune ordinals after filtering, not Unicode character offsets or image coordinates. Latin labels identify the runes; they are not decoded words. The alphabet array lets you recover each rune from its zero-based index without a separate lookup file. Its hash covers the UTF-8 concatenation of the runes, without separators.

Worked manuscript example: LP2-31

For LP2-31, the archived stream contains 269 runes. Its source SHA-256 is 493cb51478b106dd626ff93625abaf10c9675ad221896b5206809041dfd55b68.

Window lengthTotal windowsDistinct patterns occurring at least twice
226833
32670

The first three entries in the bigram report each occur three times. The script sorts by descending count, then by alphabet-index tuple, so ties have a reproducible order:

Rune labelsIndicesStarts
R–E4, 1884, 162, 233
H–O8, 362, 131, 224
D–S23, 157, 14, 41

These are selected rows from the full report, not an exhaustive list of repeated pairs. The empty trigram list means every three-rune window is distinct under this rule. A longer exact repeat would contain a repeated trigram, so the same stream also has no exact repeat of length greater than three. This says nothing about approximate matches, other representations, or patterns spanning multiple pages.

Find an occurrence in the original text file

Each pattern’s occurrences list maps the filtered rune positions back to the unchanged transcription. For the R–E pattern in the example above:

Start runeSource line / columnSource charactersExact source slice
844 / 20[109, 111)ᚱᛖ
1628 / 6[214, 217)ᚱ-ᛖ
23311 / 11[310, 312)ᚱᛖ

The line/column links above open the corresponding transcription row in the page record. For these three occurrences, the source line and displayed text row have been checked to agree. The highlighted row is the whole row, not a marked character range; use the column and exact slice to locate the pair. Open the manuscript reader to compare with the original image.

The second occurrence crosses a hyphen, the archive’s word-separator notation. Filtering makes these runes adjacent, but the preserved source slice keeps the separator visible. All three match the declared rune-stream rule; they would not all qualify under a rule that forbids crossing word boundaries.

source_start and source_end count Unicode characters from zero. The end is excluded: [214, 217) means characters 214, 215 and 216. source_line and source_column count from one. An LF newline starts a new source line; each Unicode character counts as one column, even if a tab or symbol takes a different visual width in an editor. These are neither UTF-8 byte offsets nor pixel positions.

To check the second occurrence directly, run this from the extracted bundle or repository:

from pathlib import Path
source = Path("text/lp2-31.txt").read_bytes().decode("utf-8")
assert source[214:217] == "ᚱ-ᛖ"
print(source.splitlines()[7])  # Source line 8; Python lists start at zero.

The JSON’s source_text field preserves the complete slice, including any intervening separators or newlines. Source-file line numbers can differ from the wiki’s displayed text-row numbers because the reader omits standalone editorial separators. Use the downloaded source file for these coordinates.

What a repeat does and does not establish

Repeated windows are observations about the selected text. Their counts alone do not give a chance probability, a cipher family or a key length. Window overlap also means that the observed windows are not independent samples. A repeated run of identical symbols illustrates the problem: several windows can be produced by one local run.

A fixed reversible alphabet substitution preserves the occurrence positions and counts of corresponding patterns, though it renames their symbols. Arbitrary transposition can change adjacency and therefore these counts. See cipher invariants before using n-grams to rank transformations.

If you compare many window lengths, page subsets or candidate transformations, record the complete search scope and any selection rule. A significance test would need a stated comparison model and must repeat the selection procedure. This guide supplies a descriptive measurement only; it does not publish a new cipher experiment or claim that a technique has solved LP2-31.

Work through a six-arrangement null-model example before assigning a chance probability to a repeat. It demonstrates both a fixed score and a score chosen after inspection.

For equal neighboring runes across LP2-00–55, see doublets and the 4–2–1 pattern. That audit includes all 86 source locations, two boundary conventions and their exact shuffle expectations.

Sources and verification

The separate LP2 trigram-repeat experiment tests an aggregate excess of matching window pairs against 999 page-preserving shuffles. It records 55 observed pairs and an upper-tail p-value of 0.799. Its result page provides a histogram, every observed repeat position, per-page CSV counts and reproduction scripts. This is a specific experiment; the general counting guide above remains applicable to other window lengths without implying those lengths have been tested.

Counting script · small-example tests · archived LP2-31 input · alphabet and page index. The worked counts were reproduced on 20 October 2026. They validate the declared calculation, not an independent transcription of the original JPEG. Follow documenting a reproducible attempt when turning a measurement into a hypothesis test.

Two repeated-marker claims: locations before interpretation

Two proposed alignments illustrate why a repeated sequence needs exact coordinates and counting rules. This audit searches the archived rune streams of LP2-00–55, retaining headings and removing non-runes. It locates markers only within pages; global positions concatenate the pages in order. All positions below begin at zero.

DJUBEI: 6395, 6389 or 6388?

The six rune labels D J U B E I occur twice under these rules:

PagePage rune intervalGlobal start
LP2-27[28, 34)6555
LP2-55[70, 76)12950

The second occurrence ends the rune stream of LP2-55. The first is followed by AE. An interval written [28, 34) includes positions 28 through 33: its end is excluded.

MeasurementCalculationResult
Start to start12950 − 65556395
Strictly between the identical six-rune markers6395 − 66389
Also exclude the AE after the first marker6395 − 76388

6388 = 4 × 1597, but that value uses the additional AE exclusion. AE is not part of the repeated six-rune marker. The identity is reproducible with that boundary; it should not be presented as the unqualified distance between the two copies. Changing the corpus, heading treatment or transcription can change global positions.

O F L OE NG: what the subtraction produces

The five-rune marker O F L OE NG occurs at LP2-30 rune 86 and LP2-52 rune 179. Align those starts and subtract the earlier page from the later page modulo 29. The following sixteen-position span is the one specified in the proposal; the audit does not search lengths or offsets for a better word.

Using zero-based rune indices gives:

F F F F F E A R TH S I G W O TH Y

The matching marker necessarily gives five zeros, represented by F. The next four output runes are E A R TH, which transliterate to EARTH. This is an arithmetic match, not an established word boundary or a validated reading of the surrounding output.

Using prime values, reducing their differences modulo 29 and interpreting each residue as a rune index instead gives:

F F F F F L J X G TH S OE A EO G B

These are different operations. Prime values are not interchangeable with alphabet indices. The comparison below keeps both representations visible; “offset” counts forward from the aligned marker start.

OffsetLP2-30LP2-52Index differencePrime difference → index label
0OOFF
1FFFF
2LLFF
3OEOEFF
4NGNGFF
5PTHEL
6REAAJ
7IATHRX
8AYTHG
9OESTH
10TYIS
11ONGOE
12EAGWA
13GNOEO
14AEIATHG
15MTYB

For example, the first position after the marker compares P (index 13, prime 43) with TH (index 2, prime 5). Index subtraction gives (2 − 13) mod 29 = 18, the index of E. Prime subtraction gives (5 − 43) mod 29 = 20, the index of L. Reversing the subtraction would be another operation again.

Reproduce the locations and arithmetic

Extract the reference-data bundle or use the repository, then run:

python scripts/repeated_marker_audit.py --check
python scripts/repeated_marker_audit.py

The script and full JSON ledger include input hashes, all marker occurrences, source character offsets, both representations and every output in the specified span. This does not reproduce the separate image-only claim that a DJUBEI alignment yields TRUTH: its exact paired intervals and operation have not been established here.

A next test should fix the alignment rule and output range before judging additional text, retain unsuccessful output, and account for the markers and operations already considered. See candidate readings and search space and bounds. Reproducing a short word does not identify a cipher or establish its chance probability.

title: Comparing patterns with chance: null models and selection
summary: Work through all six arrangements of a small example, then see how choosing a pattern changes the comparison.
html:
A repeat can be real without being unusual. To ask whether it is unusual, specify what other arrangements you are comparing it with. A null model supplies those alternatives and their probabilities. It is a mathematical comparison, not a claim that the manuscript was actually generated at random.

Start with a question the model can answer

Suppose the question is whether neighboring symbols match unusually often, given the symbols already present. Shuffling their order preserves the counts while changing adjacency. Generating fresh symbols uniformly changes both counts and order. These answer different questions.

ComparisonWhat stays fixedWhat can change
Shuffle the entire rune streamLength and each rune’s countOrder, neighboring pairs and row membership

title: What cipher operations preserve
summary: Compare rearrangements, fixed substitutions, and position-dependent shifts before choosing a measurement.
html:
An invariant is something an operation leaves unchanged. In cipher analysis, invariants help you check an implementation and avoid tests that cannot distinguish the candidates you are comparing. If every rearrangement of the same runes has the same whole-stream index of coincidence, selecting the rearrangement with the “best IoC” cannot work.

First fix what counts as a symbol

For the examples here, one symbol is one of the 29 runes, represented by its zero-based index. A label such as TH or NG still represents one rune. Keep the same input boundaries throughout a comparison: removing a heading or dropping punctuation is a preprocessing decision, not part of the substitution or rearrangement itself. See rune indices and prime values and transcription layers.

What each operation preserves

MeasurementPure transpositionFixed one-to-one substitutionPosition-dependent shifts
Number of symbolsPreservedPreservedPreserved
Count of each named runePreservedNot generally preservedNot generally preserved
Counts sorted without rune namesPreservedPreservedNot guaranteed
Whole-stream IoCPreservedPreservedNot guaranteed
Sum of fixed rune prime valuesPreservedNot generally preservedNot generally preserved
Which positions contain equal symbolsNot generally preservedPreservedNot guaranteed

“Not guaranteed” does not mean “must change.” A particular input can happen to give the same result. A fixed one-to-one substitution uses the same reversible alphabet mapping at every position; ordinary Atbash and a uniform shift are examples. A repeating Vigenère key can instead apply different shifts to different positions.

A necessary condition can constrain a model without rejecting it. For the specific nonzero-key rule Cᵢ − Cᵢ₋₁ = Kᵢ(Pᵢ − 28) mod 29, a doublet is equivalent to plaintext EA. The EA running-sum explanation proves the condition, checks all finite transitions and shows where it fails if assumptions change. The observed 86 doublets require 86 EA events at the measured within-page transitions; no plaintext distribution is inferred.

A five-rune example

Start with F F U F U, or indices 0 0 1 0 1. It has three F runes and two U runes. Its matching-pair numerator is 3 × 2 + 2 × 1 = 8; dividing by 5 × 4 = 20 gives IoC 2/5.

OperationOutput indicesIoCWhat happened
Reverse the sequence1 0 1 0 02/5The same runes occupy different positions.
Add 1 to every index1 1 2 1 22/5Three F become three U; two U become two TH.
Subtract the repeating key [0, 1]0 28 1 28 11/5The counts become 1, 2, and 2 across three runes.

The uniform shift preserves the pattern of repetitions even though it changes the rune names. The first, second, and fourth symbols are still equal. Their prime values are different, however: the original prime sum is 3 × 2 + 2 × 3 = 12, while the uniformly shifted sum is 3 × 3 + 2 × 5 = 19. IoC and a Gematria Primus sum measure different properties.

Why IoC survives alphabet relabeling

The IoC formula uses the counts, not the names attached to them. A reversible substitution merely moves those counts to different alphabet entries. Its numerator and denominator therefore stay the same. A transposition keeps each named count unchanged, so it preserves IoC for an even simpler reason.

This also holds for any statistic calculated only from the multiset of counts, such as empirical symbol entropy. It does not hold for a score that compares named rune frequencies against a particular expected distribution: that score depends on which count belongs to which rune. Nor does it automatically hold for measurements made on selected positions or separate columns, because a rearrangement can move runes across those boundaries.

Reproduce the example

Run this with Python 3. It uses exact fractions and the standard library; no data files, network, or AI calls are needed.

from collections import Counter
from fractions import Fraction

def ioc(symbols):
    n = len(symbols)
    if n < 2:
        return None
    counts = Counter(symbols)
    return Fraction(sum(v * (v - 1) for v in counts.values()), n * (n - 1))

source = [0, 0, 1, 0, 1]
reversed_order = source[::-1]
uniform_shift = [(c + 1) % 29 for c in source]
key = [0, 1]
varying_shift = [(c - key[i % len(key)]) % 29 for i, c in enumerate(source)]

for name, symbols in [
    ("original", source),
    ("reversed", reversed_order),
    ("uniform", uniform_shift),
    ("varying", varying_shift),
]:
    print(name, symbols, ioc(symbols))

assert Counter(source) == Counter(reversed_order)
assert sorted(Counter(source).values()) == sorted(Counter(uniform_shift).values())
assert ioc(source) == ioc(reversed_order) == ioc(uniform_shift) == Fraction(2, 5)
assert ioc(varying_shift) == Fraction(1, 5)

Choose a test that can change

For a transposition search, length and rune counts are integrity checks. To compare candidate orders, examine something sensitive to order, such as repeated neighboring pairs, the distribution within specified columns, or a fully stated language score. A promising score still needs controls for how many arrangements were tried.

For fixed alphabet substitutions, global IoC cannot select the correct mapping. Rune identities and repeated-word patterns can carry information that this single number discards. For position-dependent ciphers, a change in IoC is possible but is not a proof that a key is correct. The IoC guide explains whole-stream versus column measurements; the reproduction guide explains how to record the search scope.

This matters when counting a search space: enumerating 58 shifts and orders does not give 58 different whole-stream IoC scores. Before running a large search, use a small example to check whether your chosen measurement can respond to the parameter you are changing.

What these checks establish

These are mathematical properties of the operations as defined here, illustrated with an artificial sequence. They are not newly completed experiments on an unsolved page. A proposed transposition that changes the rune counts has done something besides rearranging the fixed input; a proposal that preserves them has passed an integrity check, not proved a solution.

For a manuscript example, compare the Warning’s archived and Atbash-decoded sums: both contain 184 runes, but their prime-value totals differ.

For a concrete boundary audit, see word lengths and corpus comparisons. Counting six decimal labels as length-one tokens reconciles two manuscript summaries without changing any rune.

A finite-difference exclusion on the archived pages

A direct polynomial stream is a narrower proposal than a polynomial key combined with unknown plaintext. For c[i] ≡ P(N+s*i) (mod m), a degree-at-most-d polynomial has (d+1)st differences divisible by m. If those differences have greatest common divisor 1, no integer modulus greater than one can work.

The direct polynomial stream experiment checks degree bounds 1–8 in both index and prime coordinates on all 55 nonempty rune pages in LP2-00–55. All 880 checks have gcd 1. Its worked example, full difference ledger and two independent implementations explain the result. Origins and fixed signed strides are covered algebraically; unknown plaintext, irregular clocks, resets and extra output maps are outside this conclusion.

Repeated positions can eliminate an unknown origin

If a rune always labels a divisor q of N+s*i, then q divides the differences between its numbered positions. The position-divisor experiment finds a gcd-one gap witness on each of the 55 nonempty LP2-00–55 rune streams. That excludes unit strides for every origin. For general stride s, it only forces the witnessed divisor to divide s. A worked diagram and stride-two counterexample show why the distinction matters.

For a guide to the logical strength of these findings, see what has actually been ruled out. It distinguishes exact exclusions from necessary constraints and explains how a counterexample limits a broader claim.

Fixed affine maps of the literal prime alphabet

The full-palette affine experiment covers every integer modulus above 109. A fixed affine rule that bijectively maps all 29 literal prime values back into the same palette acts as identity. Its divisor certificate replaces an arbitrary modulus cutoff; the record includes a worked branch and counterexamples for noninjective maps and partial palettes. This does not apply to affine maps on rune indices modulo 29 or prime-derived running keys.

The page-support variant checks all nonempty LP2-00–55 rune supports. LP2-55 has two additional maps that change F to T or Y and fix its other rune values. This exception illustrates why the full-alphabet result cannot simply be applied to a smaller support. Neither map is a recovered reading.

title: Instars, cicadas and emergence
summary: The biological term, the linked Welcome and Parable passages, and the image beneath LP2-57.
html:
An instar is a developmental stage between molts. Liber Primus uses the term in the Welcome and again in the final parable, connecting inward movement, shedding and emergence. Understanding the biological term makes the comparison more precise without turning the passage into an automatic cipher instruction.

The biological term

The Amateur Entomologists' Society glossary defines an instar as an arthropod's developmental stage between molts. The first instar follows hatching; successive molts lead to later instars. The term applies to insects with both complete and incomplete metamorphosis. It is not a synonym for a cocoon, and it does not name one particular insect species.

In cicadas, a nymph lives underground before emerging and undergoing the final molt into a winged adult. Purdue Extension's account of periodical cicadas describes nymphs leaving the soil, climbing a support and shedding their last shell. Its 13- and 17-year examples concern periodical cicadas; the word “instar” does not itself imply either duration.

Thirteen or seventeen years is not an instar count

The numbers 13 and 17 refer to the year-based life cycles of periodical cicadas, not to thirteen or seventeen developmental stages. An instar describes a stage between molts; a life-cycle duration describes elapsed time. Purdue Entomology’s cicada account distinguishes periodical and annual cicadas and describes the final emergence and molt. Its references to a particular spring and Brood X concern that emergence event, not a current-year forecast.

StatementWhat it identifies
A 17-year periodical cicadaA life-cycle duration, not the number of times the animal molts.
An instarA developmental stage, not a fixed number of years.
An exuviaThe discarded covering after a molt, not the stage or its duration.

Both 13 and 17 are prime integers. That provides a mathematical association with primality, but the known instar passages do not specify either number as a key. The biological fact, the arithmetic property and a proposed cipher operation are three separate claims.

For example, choosing a repeating key of length 13 would still leave its thirteen values unspecified. Choosing a constant shift of 13 would be a different operation; treating 13 as a prime ordinal would select the 13th prime, 41, rather than the value 13. State which meaning is intended before testing. See prime values and ordinal positions and bounded experiment specifications.

Where the manuscript uses it

Keep three things separate while reading: a stage of development, the act of shedding, and the material left behind. The manuscript’s metaphor draws on this general setting, but these biological terms do not name the same thing.

PassageContextual EnglishSurrounding idea

title: Four unreasonable things and Lewis Carroll
summary: LP1-09 compared with the White Queen: doing versus believing, four versus six, and the limits of the association.
html:
The instruction at the end of Liber Primus's first koan can be compared with the White Queen's impossible-things speech in Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass. The comparison concerns a numbered practice that challenges ordinary expectations. It is a possible literary association, not an established quotation or source attribution.

Compare the actual words

SourceWording
LP1-09, contextual EnglishDO FOUR UNREASONABLE THINGS EACH DAY
Carroll, chapter V, “Wool and Water”Why, sometimes I've believed as many as six impossible things before breakfast.

Carroll's sentence is spoken by the White Queen in Through the Looking-Glass. The primary text at Project Gutenberg places it in a conversation about believing something Alice considers impossible. The Queen treats belief as something improved by practice.

The manuscript's literal sequence, after joining its line wrap, is DO-FOUR-UNREASONABLE-THNGS-EACH-DAY. THINGS is contextual English for THNGS under the rune-label convention. Do not silently replace the literal sequence when investigating its numbers. See transliteration and the complete first koan.

The differences matter

  • Action: the manuscript says to do things; the Queen describes believing things.
  • Number: the manuscript gives four; Carroll gives as many as six.
  • Qualifier: unreasonable is not identical to impossible. An action can be considered unreasonable without being logically or physically impossible.
  • Time: the manuscript says each day; Carroll's example is before breakfast.
  • Voice: the manuscript presents a direct instruction, while Carroll gives a character's recollection within a comic dialogue.

Those differences prevent calling the manuscript line a verbatim Carroll quotation. The structural resemblance is worth recording, but it is less specific than the holy-life verbal parallel with Blake. This article does not establish that Carroll was the immediate source of the instruction.

Read the instruction after the story

In LP1-06–09, the master rejects the student's name, occupation, species and description of consciousness as answers to who the student is. Admission to study follows the student's inability to complete another answer. The four-things instruction comes after this exchange, separated as an instruction. A possible reading is that it extends the story's challenge to familiar explanations into a daily exercise. That is editorial interpretation, not an additional decoded message.

Carroll's scene instead concerns Alice's refusal to believe an apparently impossible age and the Queen's response. The two contexts both challenge ordinary judgments, but their immediate questions differ: identity in the koan, belief in the Carroll exchange. A similarity in tone does not demonstrate identical philosophical commitments.

What happens around the White Queen’s remark?

The sentence appears within a longer sequence of reversals in chapter V of the primary text. Reading that sequence helps distinguish a character’s comic argument from a direct instruction by the author.

Moment in the sceneWhat the dialogue does
Memory and punishmentThe Queen remembers future events and describes a messenger punished before his trial and crime. Alice challenges the order.
The broochThe Queen screams before pricking her finger. After the injury, she explains that the screaming is already finished.
Age and beliefTo distract Alice from loneliness, the Queen turns to age. Alice rejects the Queen’s claimed age of 101 years, five months and a day. The Queen responds by presenting belief as something to practise.

The impossible-things remark belongs to this last exchange. The scene repeatedly unsettles ordinary expectations about sequence and explanation. This is a reading of the scene’s structure, not evidence that the manuscript adopts the Queen’s reasoning.

How this changes the comparison with Liber Primus

In Carroll, Alice continues to question the speaker: the dialogue lets a reader notice the gap in an argument. In the first koan, the student’s difficulty answering leads to admission, and the subsequent instruction asks for action. Reading either passage as a simple endorsement of believing anything would erase those differences.

For the manuscript’s own treatment of belief, compare testing knowledge with the opening warning. The instruction to do something unreasonable and the instruction to test claims can be read together as a tension worth examining. Calling that tension intentional, or resolving it through Carroll, would require further evidence.

The Queen’s reversed sequence also does not establish a rune-reversal operation. A literary motif becomes a cipher proposal only after the input and transformation are specified below.

What would make this a cipher hypothesis?

A comparison becomes a testable cipher proposal only when it specifies an operation. “Use Carroll” leaves the text, edition, passage and transformation undetermined. A proposal would need to fix those choices, declare how punctuation and letters become rune indices, and state which manuscript positions consume the key. Record those decisions before inspecting candidate outputs.

The difference between four and six does not itself justify subtracting two from every rune, choosing a six-character key, or treating chapter V as an offset. Each would be a new assumption requiring its own scoped test. Neither the comparison here nor a search result in the wiki counts as evidence that such a technique has been tried. Use Have we tried it? for documented experiment records and the reproducibility guide for their requirements.

How to verify the comparison

  1. Open LP1-09 in the reader, then follow the complete first-koan guide to reproduce the literal reading.
  2. Open Carroll's primary text, locate chapter V and search for “six impossible things.” Read the preceding exchange as well as the famous sentence.
  3. Record both the common structure and the differences listed above. Keep an attribution claim separate from the observable wording.

Sources and status

Compare this claim with the other evidence types in referenced works and possible influences.

Manuscript evidence: LP1-09 and the compiled readings, dated to the 5 October 2026 snapshot. External text: Lewis Carroll, Through the Looking-Glass, Gutenberg edition 12, chapter V. Comparison checked on 20 October 2026. The relationship is presented as a possible association, not an authenticated influence. Related: philosophical themes.

title: The illustrated cover: compasses and Blake artwork
summary: The 1033.jpg collage, its source artworks, original download, and place in the 2014 puzzle.
html:
This is the compasses collage often reproduced as the illustrated cover of Liber Primus. Its archived filename is 1033.jpg. It appeared at an earlier stage of the 2014 puzzle, before the manuscript images catalogued here as LP1 and LP2.

Download the original JPEG · File provenance and checksum

The artwork in the collage

The image brings together details of William Blake’s works. The repeated compasses are particularly noticeable: the upper panel shows a hand working over a geometrical diagram, while the lower panel shows compasses reaching into darkness.

In his study of the 2014 image, Frank G. Bosman identifies the upper central panel as Newton, the lower central panel as The Ancient of Days, and the two side strips as details of Nebuchadnezzar. These identifications describe the source artworks; they do not by themselves establish what the puzzle authors intended the collage to mean.

For comparison, Tate’s Newton image shows the figure concentrating on a compass and scroll. The British Museum’s catalogue entry for The Ancient of Days describes the figure holding compasses from a heavenly sphere. Cropping and rearrangement matter here: inspect the source compositions before assigning a meaning to a fragment.

Why Daniel comes up in cover research

Bosman's interpretation connects all three compositions through the biblical Book of Daniel. The links are different in each case: a depicted character, a title, and a book written by the person portrayed. Follow them separately before treating the collage as one instruction.

Side panels → Nebuchadnezzar → Daniel 4
The biblical account describes the king's humiliation, life among animals, and eventual restoration. The guide compares that narrative with Blake's figure.
Lower centre → The Ancient of Days → Daniel 7
The name occurs in a vision of judgment. The passage supplies the title's background; it does not describe the compasses in Blake's composition.
Upper centre → Newton → his 1733 commentary
Newton wrote about Daniel and Revelation. The guide links his explanation of prophetic language and his discussion of the four beasts.

These are traceable connections between artworks, people, and texts. The further claim that Daniel supplies a cipher input remains a hypothesis. To make that claim testable, specify a passage and edition, the data taken from the cover, and the operation joining them. Compare the reproduced Emerson book cipher for an example where the counting rule and resulting address are available.

Where it appeared in the puzzle

The preceding Self-Reliance book cipher explains how the archived route reached this image.

The archived 2014 walkthrough places this image on the first onion site, auqgnxjtvdbll3pv.onion. The recorded HTML page title is For Every Thing That Lives Is Holy. This gives the collage another connection to Blake, alongside the closely related sentence in the manuscript’s Welcome section. See William Blake and Liber Primus for the wording in context.

The hidden message, reproduced

On 20 October 2026, default-key OutGuess extraction from this exact JPEG recovered 1,498 bytes. The extracted message begins with a greeting, supplies RSA values e and n, and contains an encrypted block labelled Crypt::RSA::ES::OAEP. The clear-signed message verified with GnuPG 2.5.21 against the recorded Cicada public key, using an isolated keyring and no legacy-digest override.

Download the full extraction · Signed message · Read the message body

The three downloads serve different purposes. The extraction preserves every recovered byte. The signed file isolates the PGP block for verification. The body is a readable derivative with PGP framing and dash escaping removed; use the signed file, not this derivative, to check the signature.

How to reproduce the extraction

Extract the reference-data ZIP and original-images ZIP into the same folder. Install OutGuess separately, then run this command from that folder. The wrapper checks the JPEG before extracting and refuses to overwrite an existing output file.

python scripts/extract_payload.py 1033 --outguess outguess --output illustrated-cover.bin

It should report 1,498 verified bytes and this SHA-256:

65ff60bfa019e424ce2ae23994f19af5692f7e12e6bc177830b42a154985defd

If OutGuess is not on your executable search path, replace the second outguess with its full path. See OutGuess extraction for the underlying operation and Running the reproduction scripts for terminal setup.

Next, follow the isolated-keyring instructions to import and check the public key. With that keyring prepared, verify this message:

gpg --no-options --homedir verify-keyring --no-auto-key-retrieve --status-fd 1 --verify exports/steganography/1033.signed.asc

The VALIDSIG line should identify 6D854CD7933322A601C3286D181F01E57A35090F. The evidence record preserves separate hashes, tool identification and the verification status output.

Continue to RSA decryption

Extracting the message does not decrypt the encrypted block. Verifying its signature establishes that the signed text matches the recorded key, not the identity of a person or the authenticity of every pixel in the JPEG. The RSA reproduction guide now recovers the historical next address from all three encrypted blocks, using published factors. It explains the envelope, arithmetic and legacy padding, with a script and recorded outputs.

Why it is separate from page 00

LP1-00 is the plain title page bearing the words Liber Primus. The collage is a different image from an earlier puzzle stage. It therefore has its own entry rather than taking a numbered place in the 75-image manuscript catalogue.

The three-image hidden-message chain uses LP1-00, LP1-01 and LP1-02. Its name can be confusing: that chain concerns the manuscript’s title pages and warning, not this compasses collage. The title-page guide explains those visible headings and hidden messages.

Check the downloaded file

The download preserves the bytes of the JPEG in the pinned community archive; it has not been resized or re-encoded. It is 1327 × 1427 pixels and 342,361 bytes. Matching this checksum confirms the archived file, not who created it.

SHA-256: 15b2b99fe15ff34ef3eab574bb84bfaad0a119674be2ca5baf65951e6a9bd865

The same original is included in the original-images ZIP. Its separate provenance record keeps it distinguishable from the numbered manuscript pages.

Testing geometric interpretations

The compass and geometric cipher guide shows why one matched index pair does not identify Atbash, how a full mapping can be checked, and which coordinates and transformation rules make an image overlay reproducible.

The preceding Self-Reliance book cipher explains how the archived route reached this image.

title: Newton: the upper compasses panel
summary: The drawing instrument, Blake’s portrayal of Newton, and how to compare the cover fragment.
html:
The upper central panel of the illustrated cover concentrates on a hand, compasses and a geometrical drawing. Frank G. Bosman’s published identification traces this fragment to William Blake’s Newton. Understanding the whole composition helps explain what the crop leaves out.

What the original depicts

Tate’s reproduction and description show Newton concentrating on a drawing while seated on a textured rock. Tate interprets his attention to the instrument and scroll, and his disregard for his surroundings, as Blake’s criticism of a view of the world confined to rational measurement. This is the museum’s account of Blake’s image, not an explanation supplied by the puzzle authors.

Here, compasses means the hinged drawing instrument used to construct circles and transfer distances. It is not a magnetic compass for finding north. That distinction matters before proposing an operation based on direction, angle or radius.

Identify the museum object

Tate’s published metadata identifies its Newton as N05058. An accession number identifies an object in a collection; it is not a date or a manuscript page number. The record gives the following details:

Date
1795–c. 1805; the “c.” means approximately.
Medium
Colour print, ink and watercolour on paper.
Support dimensions
460 × 600 mm, as recorded. These are physical dimensions, not pixel dimensions of an online image.
Acquisition credit
Presented by W. Graham Robertson, 1939.

Download the unmodified Tate metadata record, or inspect its pinned source through the source and checksum manifest. Tate labels this repository as an October 2014 dataset that is no longer maintained; it is a dated collection record, not a claim about the museum’s current display or latest cataloguing. Tate dataset documentation.

The accession identifies Tate’s object. It does not establish that this particular impression, or Tate’s digital photograph of it, supplied the puzzle fragment. Keep that question separate from recognizing the composition.

How to check the fragment

  1. Open the preserved cover JPEG and Tate’s image in separate tabs.
  2. Locate the hand, the two legs of the compasses and the drawing beneath them. Compare their arrangement, rather than matching only the general subject.
  3. Bosman describes the Newton fragment as mirrored. Check left and right against the complete work; record any reflection separately from cropping.
  4. Keep the original JPEG unchanged. If you make an annotated comparison, label it as a derivative and record the source image used.

Newton's book on Daniel and Revelation

Newton also wrote about biblical prophecy. The Newton Project records Observations upon the Prophecies of Daniel, and the Apocalypse of St. John, London, 1733. Here, Apocalypse of St. John names the biblical Book of Revelation. This is a separate work by the person Blake depicts, not a text visible in the cover fragment.

Bosman uses this book to connect the Newton panel with the other cover subjects. His post gives the date as 1773; the Newton Project's edition record gives 1733. Use the edition record when citing the work.

What Newton is interpreting

In Part I, chapter II, printed pages 16–18, Newton explains prophetic imagery through an analogy between nature and political society. In his reading, rising toward heaven can represent gaining power or honour, while earthquakes can represent kingdoms being shaken or overthrown. He is explaining figurative meanings in biblical passages. These correspondences do not establish substitutions for Liber Primus runes.

Part I, chapter IV, beginning on printed page 28, applies that approach to Daniel's four beasts. Newton reads them through a succession of empires and explicitly discusses the Son of Man approaching the Ancient of Days in judgment. This provides a specific passage to compare with Daniel 7 and the title of Blake's image.

Follow the connection one step at a time

  1. Identify the image: compare the cover fragment with Blake's Newton.
  2. Identify the historical text: consult Newton's 1733 work and record the chapter and printed page, rather than citing only its title.
  3. Compare the subjects: read the separate accounts of Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 4 and the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7.
  4. State the remaining hypothesis: these connections support discussing Daniel as a possible shared reference. They do not establish that the puzzle authors selected Newton's book as a cipher key or indexing text.

A book-cipher proposal would need to specify the edition, which parts of the book count, and how numbers select text. The book-cipher guide explains why those choices matter. The linked Newton Project chapters provide transcriptions with printed-page markers; keep those markers distinct from browser lines or PDF page numbers.

From artwork to a research question

The other central panel also contains compasses: see The Ancient of Days. Their repetition makes measurement a reasonable subject for interpretation. It does not specify a numerical cipher. A test based on the drawing would still need to say which points are measured, how image scaling is handled, and how a measurement becomes a symbol.

For the manuscript’s own language about perception and the individual, follow philosophical themes. The Blake overview treats the separate verbal parallel in Welcome.

title: Nebuchadnezzar: the cover’s side panels
summary: The biblical figure in Blake’s artwork and the distinction between identification and a proposed book source.
html:
The narrow strips beside the central compasses panels are identified as fragments of William Blake’s Nebuchadnezzar in Frank G. Bosman’s study of the cover. They are easy to overlook because the collage splits the composition into its margins.

Who is Nebuchadnezzar?

In Tate’s account of Blake’s work, the subject is the biblical king reduced to an animal-like existence as punishment for pride. Tate dates its work to 1795–about 1805 and identifies the medium as colour print with ink and watercolour on paper. The title names the figure in the artwork; it is not a word transcribed from the cover.

The episode in Daniel 4

The narrative behind the subject is more specific than a general image of a fallen king. Read Daniel 4:28–37 in the King James Version; the chapter moves through pride, loss, and restoration:

Verses 28–30: the boast
Nebuchadnezzar attributes Babylon’s greatness to his own power and majesty.
Verses 31–33: the humiliation
A heavenly pronouncement removes his kingdom. He is driven away from people, eats grass, and is exposed to dew. The description compares his hair to eagle feathers and his nails to bird claws.
Verses 34–36: the return
He looks toward heaven, regains understanding, and is restored to his kingdom.
Verse 37: the stated lesson
His closing praise identifies pride as something divine power can bring low.

The hair and nail comparisons provide concrete textual details to inspect against the full artwork. They are similes in this translation, not a statement that the king becomes a bird. The passage also continues beyond the animal-like condition to restoration; the isolated cover fragments do not show that whole sequence.

For the puzzle, keep three steps distinct: the text explains the artwork’s subject; visual correspondence supports identifying the borrowed composition; a further argument would be needed to make Daniel a cipher source. Selecting this translation for a readable reference does not establish that the puzzle authors used it. A book-cipher test would need an edition and counting rule as well as a passage.

Identify the museum object

Tate’s published metadata identifies its Nebuchadnezzar as N05059. An accession number identifies an object in a collection; it is not a date or a manuscript page number. The record gives the following details:

Date
1795–c. 1805; the “c.” means approximately.
Medium
Colour print, ink and watercolour on paper.
Support dimensions
543 × 725 mm, as recorded. These are physical dimensions, not pixel dimensions of an online image.
Acquisition credit
Presented by W. Graham Robertson, 1939.

Download the unmodified Tate metadata record, or inspect its pinned source through the source and checksum manifest. Tate labels this repository as an October 2014 dataset that is no longer maintained; it is a dated collection record, not a claim about the museum’s current display or latest cataloguing. Tate dataset documentation.

The accession identifies Tate’s object. It does not establish that this particular impression, or Tate’s digital photograph of it, supplied the puzzle fragment. Keep that question separate from recognizing the composition.

How to inspect the side panels

Begin with the unchanged cover image and the full composition shown by Tate. Follow the outlines of the limbs and hair through each narrow strip. Bosman describes rotated fragments; compare orientation as well as shape. A fragment can become difficult to recognize when a familiar horizontal body is turned into a vertical border.

Record which source reproduction you compare. Different photographs and impressions can differ in colour, contrast and framing. Identifying the composition is a different task from identifying the exact digital image used to assemble the collage.

Why the Book of Daniel enters the discussion

The book-cipher guide explains what must be specified before a proposed book source becomes a reproducible lookup.

Bosman develops a proposed Daniel connection from the cover’s imagery. That is an interpretive argument, not a reproduced book-cipher result. Recognizing Nebuchadnezzar explains why someone might investigate a biblical source; it does not select a passage, translation or indexing rule.

If you pursue that idea, the experiment-writing guide explains how to state those choices before testing. Keep the artwork identification and the proposed cipher test as separate claims so another reader can accept one without being asked to accept the other.

Return to the cover overview, or compare the central panels: Newton and The Ancient of Days.

The companion Daniel 7 reference locates the name Ancient of Days and distinguishes the vision from Blake’s figure with compasses.

title: The Ancient of Days: the lower compasses panel
summary: The frontispiece, the figure with compasses, and why the exact Blake copy matters.
html:
The lower central panel of the compasses cover is identified as a detail of William Blake’s The Ancient of Days by Frank G. Bosman’s cover study. The complete composition supplies context that is lost when the hand and instrument are isolated.

What is a frontispiece?

A frontispiece is an illustration placed at the beginning of a book. The British Museum’s record for Europe: a Prophecy, copy A, plate 1 identifies this design as its frontispiece. The catalogue describes a bearded figure in a luminous sphere, extending compasses into the darkness below. It gives the figure’s identity as probably Urizen; that qualification should remain when citing the record.

The collection record describes a particular copy. A work title alone does not identify which impression, colouring or modern reproduction was used in the puzzle image. This entry does not establish that the collage was made from the museum’s copy A.

Which museum object is linked?

Catalogue fieldBritish Museum record
Registration number1936,1116.32
Work and positionEurope: a Prophecy, copy A, plate 1
Production1794; published in London
Process and inkRelief and white-line etching, printed in blue-green ink
Catalogued dimensions234 × 168 mm

The museum’s curator notes describe copy A as an early, incomplete proof: eleven plates on eight leaves, with almost no hand-colouring. They separately give approximate sheet dimensions of 332 × 262 mm. These are physical dimensions, not pixel sizes for a downloaded image.

The registration number identifies this collection object; its opening year is not the work’s production date. Keep the copy, plate, date, and physical dimensions attached to their catalogue labels when taking notes.

Why the copy matters to the cover comparison

The blue-green proof provides a reference for the composition, while the preserved cover fragment has a different colour appearance. That difference leaves an exact source-copy identification open. It could require comparison with other impressions or reproductions, as well as any changes made while assembling the collage. The linked record alone does not decide between those possibilities.

A useful comparison record names both images, marks corresponding contours, and records any crop, rotation, reflection, or colour adjustment. Matching the hand and instrument can support identification of the design. Identifying one particular reproduction requires finer evidence, such as matching print detail or image defects. Use original-image coordinates to make those comparisons inspectable.

How to compare the cover

  1. Open the original cover and the museum’s complete design.
  2. Trace the hand and the two legs of the instrument. Compare their relationship to the surrounding light and the partly visible head.
  3. Check the orientation: Bosman describes a rotated fragment. Record the rotation and crop separately instead of treating a transformed image as a different drawing.
  4. To identify an exact source copy, compare small distinctive details and colour placement across documented copies, not merely the common outline.

The name in Daniel 7

The phrase appears in Daniel 7:9–14, here linked in the King James Version. This is a judgment scene in a vision, distinct from Nebuchadnezzar’s episode in chapter 4.

Verses 9–10
The Ancient of Days is seated, with white clothing and hair compared to wool. The throne, wheels, and a stream are described through fire. A multitude attends, judgment is set, and books are opened.
Verses 13–14
A figure described as like the Son of man approaches with the clouds and comes before the Ancient of Days. Dominion and an enduring kingdom are granted.

These verses supply a location for the name and its surrounding imagery. They do not describe a figure extending compasses from a luminous sphere. That distinction matters when moving from a title to the details of Blake’s composition.

A biblical title and a Blake character

Keep the title’s textual background separate from the identification of the figure. The museum record above calls the figure probably Urizen; the Urizen guide explains that character’s role in Blake. Neither label makes the frontispiece a literal illustration of every detail in Daniel’s vision.

Bosman’s cover interpretation brings the title and Nebuchadnezzar together through Daniel. Readers can now inspect both passages directly. This is a checkable literary connection, but it still leaves the puzzle authors’ purpose and any proposed book-cipher operation to be demonstrated separately.

What the repeated instrument tells us

Newton, in the upper panel, also supplies a hand with compasses. The collage therefore places two acts of measurement together. Reading that arrangement as a theme is different from extracting a key from it: a cipher proposal needs an explicit rule that someone else can apply to the same source bytes.

See Nebuchadnezzar for the side panels and the proposed Daniel connection, and William Blake and Liber Primus for the manuscript’s textual allusion.

For the terminology behind these comparisons, see Blake prints: plates, impressions, and copies. Its illustrated explanation separates the printing method from the identity of a particular source image.

title: Decrypting the illustrated cover’s RSA message
summary: Reproduce the three historical RSA blocks and understand the Crypt::RSA 1.99 padding difference.
html:
The 1033.jpg cover hides a signed message containing an RSA public key and encrypted data. This guide reproduces the historical decryption using published factors. It recovers a navigation address from the 2014 puzzle; it does not solve an unknown manuscript page.

Run the reproduction

Extract the reference-data ZIP. From the extracted folder, run:

python scripts/reproduce_cover_rsa.py

The script needs only Python 3’s standard library. It reads the included verified message body and makes no network requests. Its output lists three blocks, their recovered bytes and successful RSA round-trip checks. The complete plaintext is:

\ncu343l33nqaekrnw.onion\n\n

Here \n denotes a newline byte. The address is historical output, not a service contacted by this reproduction. Download the recorded result or inspect the script.

What the key numbers mean

The signed body gives e = 65537 and a modulus n. The modulus is the integer that defines the range of RSA arithmetic; this one is 432 bits long. The public exponent e specifies the public modular-power operation. To undo it, this reproduction uses two published factors, p and q, whose product equals n.

Connor Tumbleson’s reconstruction supplies those factors. The script checks their product against the modulus read from the message, calculates phi = (p - 1)(q - 1), and obtains the private exponent as the modular inverse d = e⁻¹ mod phi. Supplying the factors avoids repeating factor discovery. The fast runtime of this script therefore says nothing about how long factoring took.

For a small worked example of that calculation, see the totient and RSA. It explains why the factors must be distinct primes and how a modular inverse differs from division.

Unwrap the message in the right order

  1. Base64: decode the printable encrypted block into bytes.
  2. Checksum: compare the attached MD5 value with the compressed bytes. This is the historical format’s integrity check, not a substitute for the PGP signature.
  3. Compression: decompress the zlib stream.
  4. Content frame: read the length-prefixed field named Cyphertext, preserving that spelling. It holds 162 bytes: three 54-byte RSA blocks.
  5. RSA: for each ciphertext integer c, calculate m = cᵈ mod n. Re-encrypt m and require the original c.
  6. Padding: decode the legacy OAEP structure and concatenate the three recovered message fragments.

Why an ordinary OAEP decoder can fail

OAEP adds structured padding before RSA encryption. Recovering the modular integer is only part of decryption; the padding must also be decoded using the same rules as the sender.

The message names Crypt::RSA::ES::OAEP, version 1.99. In that release’s DataFormat.pm, the SHA-1 mask generator uses counters 0, 20, 40 and so on. Standard MGF1 advances by one instead. This small implementation difference changes the mask bytes and causes a standard decoder to reject this message’s padding. The reproduction follows the named legacy implementation and checks the empty-label hash and padding delimiter in every block.

On 20 October 2026, a separate PyCryptodome 3.23.0 OAEP decoder with the legacy mask rule matched all three fragments. Its default mask rejected all three. This is a compatibility finding about this historical message, not a reason to use these old rules for new encryption.

Sources and scope

title: Emerson’s Self-Reliance and the opening book cipher
summary: The essay’s documented place in the 2014 route, a first-coordinate example, and comparisons with Liber Primus.
html:
Ralph Waldo Emerson’s Self-Reliance belongs in the history of the 2014 puzzle for a specific reason: the archived opening route uses it as a book-cipher source. It also offers useful comparisons with Liber Primus’s treatment of inward knowledge and conformity. Those are two different connections, with different kinds of evidence.

Its place before the illustrated cover

The pinned 2014 walkthrough identifies Emerson’s essay as the source indicated by the opening riddle. It records a four-part lookup rule: paragraph, sentence, word, letter. The reported result is auqgnxjtvdbll3pv.onion, the historical site that displayed the 1033.jpg compasses collage.

This places the essay before the cover’s RSA message. The two addresses belong to successive steps; they are not conflicting solutions to the same clue. Neither address is contacted by the site’s reproduction scripts.

Follow the first coordinate

The walkthrough points to this Dartmouth-hosted PDF of Self-Reliance. The first coordinate is 1:2:3:1. Count from the first prose paragraph, after the title and opening verse. Its second sentence begins The soul always. The third word is always, whose first letter is a. This agrees with the first character of the reported address.

Reproduce all the lookups

The complete replay was checked on 20 October 2026. Extract the reference-data ZIP and run:

python scripts/reproduce_emerson.py

This uses Python’s standard library and the included paragraph derivative. It prints the complete result and every selected sentence, word and character. The output is auqgnxjtvdbll3pv.onion; no network request is made.

For a second level of reproduction, install pypdf==6.19.0 in your Python environment and run python scripts/reproduce_emerson.py --check-pdf. This re-extracts the included source PDF and compares all 50 derived paragraphs before doing the lookups. The default command does not require that package.

3:3:13:5geniusu
